title: ADP Value and Reaching vs Falling (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: ADP Value (Reaching vs Falling). SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The gap between a player's market average draft position and your own projected rank, signaling whether the field is over- or under-pricing him. INPUTS (general): player projections, public ADP, current draft slot. HOW TO READ IT: A player whose projected rank sits well ahead of his ADP is a value (let him fall); one taken far before his ADP is a reach. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to time picks and capture surplus instead of drafting strict best-player-available off a single ranking; beats taking your favorite name a full round early. COMMON MISTAKE: Reaching for a target you could have gotten a round later, burning the value the ADP gap was telling you to exploit. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Zero-RB Construction (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Zero-RB Construction. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/PPR; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: A roster-build strategy that fades early running backs to load up on high-floor pass-catchers, then mines RB production from value and the waiver wire later. INPUTS (general): positional injury attrition, projected target volume, draft slot. HOW TO READ IT: Strong when WR/TE scoring is dense and RB injury risk is high; the build leans on contingent backs hitting in-season. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use in deeper PPR leagues to dodge fragile early-RB outcomes; beats reflexively spending the first three picks on running backs. COMMON MISTAKE: Going Zero-RB without a plan to acquire volume backs later, leaving a permanent hole at the position. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Robust-RB Construction (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Robust-RB Construction. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: A build that front-loads multiple running backs early to corner a scarce, high-leverage position before it dries up. INPUTS (general): positional scarcity curve, projected RB workload, draft slot. HOW TO READ IT: Strong when the RB tier cliff is steep and waiver-wire RB replacement is unreliable. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use in standard or shallow leagues where startable RBs are scarce; beats spreading early picks thin across positions that replenish more easily. COMMON MISTAKE: Over-committing to RB in a year of deep RB supply, leaving the WR and TE corps weak. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Late-Round QB (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Late-Round QB. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: A timing strategy that waits on quarterback because the weekly scoring gap between mid-tier and elite QBs is small relative to their draft cost. INPUTS (general): positional replacement level, projected QB scoring spread, draft slot. HOW TO READ IT: Strong in single-QB formats where streamable passers approximate elite output at a fraction of the price. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to spend premium capital on scarce RB/WR and grab QB late; beats reaching for a top QB in the early rounds in 1QB leagues. COMMON MISTAKE: Applying it in SuperFlex/2QB leagues, where QB scarcity flips and waiting becomes a trap. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Handcuff Value (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Handcuff Value. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The insurance value of drafting the direct backup to a starting running back, who inherits a featured workload if the starter is hurt. INPUTS (general): starter injury risk, backup's projected inherited role, depth-chart clarity. HOW TO READ IT: High when the backup would step into a clear lead role; low in committee backfields where the touches would scatter. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to protect a fragile early RB investment or speculate on standalone-plus-contingent upside; beats leaving a high-pick RB uninsured. COMMON MISTAKE: Handcuffing your own star too early instead of taking the highest-leverage backups across the league. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Contingent-Upside Lottery Backs (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Contingent-Upside (Lottery-Ticket Backs). SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The conditional ceiling of a buried back whose value is near-zero in the base case but league-winning if a single event (injury, depth-chart shift) unlocks a featured role. INPUTS (general): path-to-touches probability, projected role if promoted, draft cost. HOW TO READ IT: Read it as an option value: low expected points but a fat right tail worth a late-round dart. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use late and in bulk to buy cheap exposure to high-variance outcomes; beats spending the same late picks on flat, capped veterans. COMMON MISTAKE: Pricing the lottery ticket like a starter and drafting it rounds too early. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Rookie Draft Capital Valuation (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Rookie Draft-Capital Valuation. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a rookie's real-NFL draft slot predicts opportunity and fantasy outcome, since teams feed early-capital players touches and targets. INPUTS (general): NFL draft position, projected landing-spot role, positional age curve. HOW TO READ IT: High NFL draft capital signals an invested team and a likely path to volume; late capital signals a steeper climb. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to separate rookie hype from durable opportunity; beats ranking rookies on college stats or highlight reputation alone. COMMON MISTAKE: Ignoring landing spot, so a high-capital rookie stuck behind entrenched starters gets over-drafted. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Target-Share Projection (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Target-Share Projection. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/PPR; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: A receiver's projected fraction of his team's total targets, the most stable upstream driver of PPR scoring. INPUTS (general): historical target share, projected role and depth-chart change, team pass volume. HOW TO READ IT: A high projected share signals dependable volume; a low share signals reliance on efficiency or touchdowns that regress. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to anchor WR/TE projections in repeatable usage; beats valuing pass-catchers off prior-year fantasy points, which bake in volatile efficiency. COMMON MISTAKE: Confusing raw catches with share, missing that a target share on a low-volume offense yields fewer looks. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Opportunity Share and Volume (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Opportunity Share (Total Volume). SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: A back's combined share of team carries plus targets, capturing total touch volume that drives fantasy floor more than per-touch efficiency. INPUTS (general): projected carry share, projected target share, team play volume. HOW TO READ IT: High opportunity share means a back accrues points on volume regardless of efficiency swings; low share means he needs big plays to score. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to find floor-stable RBs and to value pass-catching backs in PPR; beats ranking RBs on yards-per-carry, which is noisy and unstable year to year. COMMON MISTAKE: Crediting a strong rushing share while ignoring that a back ceded all third-down and goal-line work. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Air Yards and aDOT for Valuation (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Air Yards and aDOT. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The total downfield yardage a receiver is thrown and his average depth of target, capturing the size and shape of his receiving opportunity beyond catches. INPUTS (general): projected air-yards volume, average depth of target, target share. HOW TO READ IT: High air yards signal big-play and touchdown equity; a deep aDOT means a higher ceiling but a lower, spikier floor. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to spot receivers whose underlying opportunity outruns their box-score points; beats valuing WRs on receptions alone, which underrates field-stretchers. COMMON MISTAKE: Chasing raw air yards without weighing efficiency, drafting a deep threat whose volume never converts. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Red-Zone Opportunity (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Red-Zone Opportunity. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: A player's share of his team's touches and targets inside the opponent's red zone, the high-leverage zone where touchdowns are scored. INPUTS (general): projected red-zone touch/target share, team red-zone trips, goal-line role. HOW TO READ IT: A high red-zone share signals durable touchdown equity; a low share warns that current scoring leans on long, unrepeatable plays. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to forecast touchdown floors and find goal-line specialists; beats projecting touchdowns off last year's total, which regresses hard. COMMON MISTAKE: Assuming a player keeps a goal-line role after a personnel change that hands those carries to someone else. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Touchdown Regression Candidates (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Touchdown Regression Candidates. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: Players whose prior-year touchdown rate diverged from their underlying opportunity, flagging likely positive or negative regression in the coming year. INPUTS (general): prior touchdown total, expected touchdowns from opportunity, projected role continuity. HOW TO READ IT: Scoring above expected opportunity flags negative regression (a fade); scoring below flags positive regression (a buy). WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to find buy-low and sell-high targets at ADP; beats projecting next year off raw fantasy points that overweight fluky scoring. COMMON MISTAKE: Treating regression as guaranteed and ignoring that an elite role can sustain an above-expected rate. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Positional Age Curves (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Positional Age Curves. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The typical performance arc by position with age, since running backs peak and decline early while receivers and quarterbacks hold value longer. INPUTS (general): player age, positional aging shape, projected role. HOW TO READ IT: A back past his positional peak carries downside risk; an aging receiver or QB in a stable role retains value further out. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to discount older RBs and to avoid overpaying for cliff-risk; beats valuing players purely on last season without an aging prior. COMMON MISTAKE: Applying one aging curve to all positions, fading a 30-year-old WR as if he were a 30-year-old RB. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Landing Spot and Role Change (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Landing Spot (Role Change). SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a player's new team, scheme, and depth chart reshape his projected opportunity after a trade, signing, or coaching change. INPUTS (general): new-team target/touch competition, scheme tendencies, projected role. HOW TO READ IT: A clear path to volume in a high-pace pass-friendly offense raises value; crowded depth charts or run-heavy schemes suppress it. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to re-rank players who changed situations rather than carrying over last year's value; beats projecting from prior usage in a different system. COMMON MISTAKE: Anchoring to a player's old role and ignoring that opportunity is environment-dependent. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: QB-WR Stacking Value (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: QB-WR Stacking Value. SPORT: Fantasy Football (best-ball/tournament; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The correlation benefit of rostering a quarterback together with his pass-catcher, so a big passing day scores twice on your team. INPUTS (general): intra-team scoring correlation, projected pass volume, format payout structure. HOW TO READ IT: High value in ceiling-seeking formats where correlated spikes win weeks; muted in points-only formats that reward stability. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use in best-ball and tournaments to raise team ceiling; beats picking the QB and WR independently as if their scores were unrelated. COMMON MISTAKE: Over-stacking in a redraft cash league where correlation adds variance without a payout for ceiling. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Bye-Week Stacking Avoidance (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Bye-Week Stacking Avoidance. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: Roster concentration risk from drafting too many starters who share the same bye week, forcing a single crippled lineup week. INPUTS (general): players' bye weeks, starter concentration by position, roster depth. HOW TO READ IT: A cluster of key starters on one bye week is a red flag; spread byes signal a manageable schedule. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use as a late-round tiebreaker between similar players to smooth weekly lineups; beats ignoring byes and fielding a hollow team on a single week. COMMON MISTAKE: Letting bye-week avoidance override value, passing a clearly better player to dodge a manageable overlap. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Positional Run Dynamics (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Positional Run Dynamics (Tier Runs). SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The cascade when several drafters take the same position in quick succession, draining a tier and shifting scarcity in real time. INPUTS (general): live positional supply by tier, opponents' roster needs, draft slot. HOW TO READ IT: An active run signals a tier is about to empty; reading it tells you whether to join the run or pivot to an untouched position. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to anticipate scarcity and grab the last player in a tier before the cliff; beats drafting in a vacuum off a static ranking. COMMON MISTAKE: Panic-joining a run and reaching for a lesser player when an untapped position offered better value. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Value-Based Drafting Variants (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Value-Based Drafting Variants. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The family of baselines used to convert projections into cross-position value, differing by how the replacement reference is defined (last-starter, worst-starter, or blended baselines). INPUTS (general): player projections, choice of replacement baseline, league starter requirements. HOW TO READ IT: Each baseline reshapes which position looks scarce; a steeper baseline pushes value toward thin positions. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to pick a baseline that matches your league's roster rules; beats comparing raw projected points across positions that play by different supply. COMMON MISTAKE: Adopting one baseline blindly and not realizing it systematically over- or under-rates a position for your settings. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Floor vs Ceiling Consistency (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Floor vs Ceiling (Consistency). SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The week-to-week distribution of a player's outcomes, separating high-floor consistency from high-ceiling upside at the same projected average. INPUTS (general): projected mean, outcome variance, role stability. HOW TO READ IT: A high floor means dependable startable weeks; a high ceiling means spike potential with more bust risk. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use floor players to stabilize a strong roster and ceiling players to chase upside when behind; beats ranking on projected average alone, which hides distribution shape. COMMON MISTAKE: Filling every slot with low-ceiling floor players, building a team with no path to a blow-up week. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Strength of Schedule for Draft (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Strength of Schedule for Draft. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The aggregate difficulty of a player's upcoming matchups, especially weighted toward the fantasy playoff weeks, as a draft-day tiebreaker. INPUTS (general): opponent defensive strength by position, schedule timing, playoff-week matchups. HOW TO READ IT: A soft schedule, particularly late, is a modest tailwind; a brutal slate is a mild fade among comparable players. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use as a thin-margin tiebreaker and to weight playoff-week matchups; beats over-trusting full-season SOS when early projections of defenses are noisy. COMMON MISTAKE: Over-drafting on SOS, treating preseason defensive rankings as reliable when they shift through the year. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Dead-Zone RB Avoidance (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Dead-Zone RB. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: A middle-round band of running backs whose ADP outpaces their expected production because they combine moderate cost with committee or injury-fragile roles. INPUTS (general): mid-round RB role ambiguity, ADP cost, opportunity-share projection. HOW TO READ IT: Backs in this band are priced like starters but profile like fliers; flagging the zone tells you where to fade. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to route mid-round capital to WRs or QBs and grab RB upside cheaper later; beats reflexively filling RB in the dead-zone band because the position feels thin. COMMON MISTAKE: Confusing a genuine value back with a dead-zone trap just because both sit in the same rounds. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Onesie Position Timing TE/QB (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Onesie Position Timing (TE/QB). SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: When to draft single-roster-slot positions like tight end and quarterback, where a small elite tier creates a real edge but the rest are nearly interchangeable. INPUTS (general): positional scoring spread, size of the elite tier, draft slot. HOW TO READ IT: If the elite tier is small and far ahead, paying up early is justified; if the position is flat after the top names, wait. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to decide between an early elite onesie and a late streaming approach; beats treating TE and QB with the same timing every year regardless of tier shape. COMMON MISTAKE: Reaching for the fourth-best onesie, paying a premium for a player barely above replacement. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Best-Ball vs Managed Valuation (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Best-Ball vs Managed Valuation. SPORT: Fantasy Football (best-ball; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How player value shifts when lineups auto-optimize with no in-season management, rewarding spike weeks and removing the cost of bye weeks and busts. INPUTS (general): outcome variance, spike-week frequency, roster depth needs. HOW TO READ IT: Ceiling and correlation gain value; consistency and bye-week planning lose importance versus managed redraft. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to re-rank for best-ball by leaning into upside and stacks; beats importing managed-league rankings that overvalue floor and waiver-dependent players. COMMON MISTAKE: Drafting best-ball like redraft, fading high-variance ceiling players the format is built to reward. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Stars-and-Scrubs vs Balanced Budget (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Auction Budget Allocation (Stars-and-Scrubs vs Balanced). SPORT: Fantasy Football (auction; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How to distribute a fixed auction budget, contrasting spending big on a few elite players and filling with minimums against spreading evenly for roster balance. INPUTS (general): total budget, positional value tiers, roster slots to fill. HOW TO READ IT: Stars-and-scrubs maximizes top-end talent but thins depth; a balanced spread buys reliability across the lineup. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use stars-and-scrubs when the elite tier is league-winning and waiver depth is strong; beats spending uniformly when a few players are clearly worth a premium. COMMON MISTAKE: Going stars-and-scrubs and running out of budget, fielding too many dollar-tier scrubs in starting slots. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Auction Nomination Strategy (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Auction Nomination Strategy. SPORT: Fantasy Football (auction; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The tactical use of who you put up for bid to drain rivals' budgets, set price anchors, and steer the market toward players you want cheap. INPUTS (general): opponents' remaining budgets, positional scarcity state, your own targets. HOW TO READ IT: Nominating players you do not want forces rivals to spend; holding your targets until budgets thin lets you buy at a discount. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use throughout the auction to manage the room's purchasing power; beats nominating your own targets early and inviting bidding wars. COMMON MISTAKE: Nominating a player you secretly want, then getting stuck overpaying when the bidding heats up. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Snap-Share Trend (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Snap-Share Trend. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The direction and slope of a player's percentage of offensive snaps across recent weeks, treated as a leading indicator of opportunity. INPUTS (general): per-game snap counts, team offensive play volume, recency weighting. HOW TO READ IT: A rising snap share signals an expanding role and a future scoring floor; a flat-but-high share confirms entrenchment; a falling share warns of a phasing-out before box-score output drops. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use for start/sit confidence and early waiver claims; it beats reacting only to last week's fantasy points, which lag role change by a week or two. COMMON MISTAKE: Treating raw snap count as role without dividing by team play volume, so a slow-paced team's starter looks under-used. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Target-Share Trend (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Target-Share Trend. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The fraction of a team's pass attempts directed at a given receiver over recent weeks, tracking how the passing game is being distributed. INPUTS (general): individual targets, team pass attempts, recency weighting. HOW TO READ IT: A high and stable target share is the most repeatable receiver signal; a climbing share flags an ascending role even before catches convert; a collapsing share precedes fantasy decline. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to rank pass-catchers for start/sit and to identify add targets; it beats receptions or yards alone, which are noisier and catch-rate dependent. COMMON MISTAKE: Ignoring that target share shrinks when a team runs more, so a back-end receiver on a run-heavy team is penalized unfairly versus per-pass rate. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Air-Yards and aDOT Trend (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Air-Yards and aDOT Trend. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The depth and volume of intended passing yards aimed at a receiver, capturing downfield opportunity independent of whether the ball was caught. INPUTS (general): air yards per target, average depth of target, share of team air yards. HOW TO READ IT: High air-yards share signals big-play upside and ceiling; a low aDOT with high volume signals a safer floor but capped ceiling; a sudden aDOT spike hints at a changed route assignment. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to separate ceiling from floor in start/sit and to find buy-low deep threats; it beats raw yardage, which conflates volume with luck on contested deep shots. COMMON MISTAKE: Chasing air yards on a player who never converts them, mistaking unrealized opportunity for guaranteed production. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Red-Zone Usage Trend (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Red-Zone Usage Trend. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: A player's share of carries and targets inside scoring range, isolating the touchdown-equity portion of a role from total-yardage usage. INPUTS (general): red-zone carries and targets, inside-the-ten opportunities, team red-zone trip volume. HOW TO READ IT: High red-zone usage predicts touchdown rate and stabilizes scoring; a player with yards but no red-zone work has a fragile, big-play-dependent line. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to value touchdown-leverage players for start/sit and to anticipate scoring regression; it beats season touchdown count, which is noisy and lags opportunity. COMMON MISTAKE: Crediting a back with goal-line value when a separate short-yardage specialist actually gets the inside-the-five carries. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Vegas Implied Team Total (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Vegas Implied Team Total. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The number of points a team is expected to score, derived from the betting market's game total and spread, used as a proxy for the size of the fantasy scoring pie. INPUTS (general): game total, point spread, home/away context. HOW TO READ IT: A high implied total lifts every skill player's expected output; a low implied total caps even good usage; the gap between the two teams' totals shapes who scores. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use as a fast environment filter for start/sit and streaming; it beats raw season averages, which ignore this week's expected scoring environment. COMMON MISTAKE: Applying the total uniformly across positions, ignoring that game flow channels it toward different player types. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Weather Adjustment (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Weather Adjustment. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The expected dampening of passing and kicking output from adverse field conditions, applied as a tilt toward the run and toward lower-variance outcomes. INPUTS (general): wind, precipitation, temperature, dome/outdoor flag. HOW TO READ IT: High wind suppresses deep passing and field goals most; heavy precipitation lowers totals and shifts volume to the run; domes and mild conditions need no adjustment. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to fade pass-game ceilings and kickers and to lean into volume backs for start/sit; it beats ignoring conditions, which over-starts deep threats in bad weather. COMMON MISTAKE: Over-fading entire games for moderate cold, when only sustained high wind reliably moves passing output. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Streaming DST (Defense) (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Streaming DST. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The weekly attractiveness of a freely available team defense, driven mostly by the quality and situation of the offense it faces rather than the defense's own talent. INPUTS (general): opponent offense quality, opponent turnover propensity, game environment (spread/total). HOW TO READ IT: Defenses facing weak, turnover-prone, or trailing offenses are top streams; sack-and-takeaway upside compounds when the opponent must pass from behind. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to rotate a one-week defense off waivers; it beats holding a brand-name defense in a bad matchup, since matchup dominates DST scoring. COMMON MISTAKE: Streaming on defensive reputation instead of the opposing offense, the larger driver of fantasy defense points. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Streaming Quarterback (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Streaming Quarterback. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The weekly value of a replaceable quarterback, weighting matchup softness and a rushing component that raises the floor independent of passing matchup. INPUTS (general): opponent pass defense, implied team total, quarterback rushing tendency. HOW TO READ IT: A mobile quarterback in a high-total game is the safest stream; a pocket passer needs both a soft matchup and a strong supporting cast to clear; low totals cap even good passers. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to fill a one-quarterback league weekly without rostering a stud; it beats fixed-rank streaming, which ignores rushing floor and game environment. COMMON MISTAKE: Chasing last week's passing-yard line while ignoring that rushing upside, not passing volume, drives the streamer floor. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Streaming Tight End (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Streaming Tight End. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The weekly value of a borderline tight end at a position where baseline scoring is low, so a single matchup edge or red-zone role can outscore the replacement pool. INPUTS (general): route participation, opponent tight-end defense, red-zone target role. HOW TO READ IT: A tight end who runs routes on most dropbacks and draws red-zone looks against a soft coverage is a top stream; low route share means touchdown-or-bust. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to cover a thin tight-end slot weekly; it beats holding a touchdown-dependent name, since route volume plus matchup is more repeatable. COMMON MISTAKE: Streaming a tight end on name value despite a route share too low to guarantee involvement. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Matchup-Based Start/Sit Edge (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Matchup-Based Start/Sit Edge. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The adjustment to a player's baseline projection from the specific defense and alignment he faces, isolating matchup from talent. INPUTS (general): opponent defensive efficiency by position, alignment/coverage tendencies, pace context. HOW TO READ IT: A large positive matchup edge promotes a borderline starter; a large negative edge benches a name player; near-zero edges defer to baseline talent and usage. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to break ties between similarly ranked players; it beats start-your-studs dogma at the margins and avoids over-starting talent into a wall. COMMON MISTAKE: Letting matchup override a clear usage and talent gap, benching an elite player for a streamer on one soft week. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Buy-Low Timing (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Buy-Low Timing. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The window where a player's trade price has dropped on poor box scores while his underlying usage and role remain strong, signaling a likely rebound. INPUTS (general): role and usage stability, recent scoring vs expected, opportunity-driven projection. HOW TO READ IT: A wide gap between strong usage and weak recent points marks a buy-low; if usage has also fallen, the discount is justified and not an opportunity. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to acquire undervalued players via trade; it beats buying on name recognition or selling low into a normal cold streak. COMMON MISTAKE: Confusing a role decline with bad luck and buying a player whose opportunity has genuinely shrunk. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Sell-High Timing (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Sell-High Timing. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The window where a player's recent scoring has outrun his sustainable usage, inflating trade value above what the role supports. INPUTS (general): touchdown rate vs opportunity, usage-based expected points, schedule difficulty ahead. HOW TO READ IT: A player scoring far above his opportunity, especially on touchdown spikes, is a sell-high; a player whose points match expanding usage is a hold. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to convert unsustainable production into durable value before regression; it beats holding every hot player until the inevitable cool-off. COMMON MISTAKE: Selling a player whose hot streak reflects a real role expansion rather than luck, giving away earned value. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Panic-Drop Avoidance (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Panic-Drop Avoidance. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether a disappointing stretch reflects a durable role loss or transient bad outcomes, used to decide whether to cut an underperformer. INPUTS (general): underlying usage stability, sample-size of the slump, replacement-level of available adds. HOW TO READ IT: Stable usage plus a small bad sample argues hold; eroded usage plus weeks of decline argues drop; the bar to drop rises when the waiver replacement is weak. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to resist cutting a held asset for a hot streamer; it beats chasing last week's points, which churns the bottom of the roster destructively. COMMON MISTAKE: Dropping a startable player after two quiet games into a tough matchup stretch, then watching the rebound on another roster. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Playoff-Schedule Streaming (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Playoff-Schedule Streaming. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The value of pre-positioning rosterable players whose fantasy-playoff-week matchups are favorable, secured before the rush. INPUTS (general): opponent strength in the playoff weeks, projected role at that time, bye-week status during playoffs. HOW TO READ IT: A player with soft playoff-week opponents and a secure role is worth stashing early even if his near-term matchups are mediocre. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to plan the title-deciding weeks rather than the next one; it beats week-to-week-only streaming, which leaves you bidding against everyone for the same names late. COMMON MISTAKE: Over-stashing for a distant matchup that injuries or depth-chart changes can erase, sacrificing too much present roster flexibility. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Handcuff Promotion on Starter Injury (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Handcuff Promotion on Starter Injury. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The expected value jump of a backup who inherits a starter's vacated workload, scaled by how much of that role and game environment transfers. INPUTS (general): vacated touches and snap share, backup's prior role, team scoring environment. HOW TO READ IT: A backup stepping into a feature, high-volume role in a good offense gains the most; a timeshare or committee inheritance gains far less. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to prioritize waiver claims the moment a starter is ruled out; it beats waiting for a confirmed box score, by which point the player is gone. COMMON MISTAKE: Assuming the backup absorbs the full role when the team actually splits the vacated work across two players. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Role Consolidation After Injury (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Role Consolidation After Injury. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: How an injury elsewhere on an offense funnels targets, carries, or red-zone work toward a remaining player, raising his ceiling beyond his own status quo. INPUTS (general): vacated opportunity at adjacent positions, the remaining player's existing role, team play-calling tendency. HOW TO READ IT: A clear primary survivor on a thinned depth chart sees concentrated usage; a crowded room dilutes the redistributed share. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to upgrade a held player or claim a beneficiary after an injury to a teammate; it beats only chasing the injured player's direct backup. COMMON MISTAKE: Ignoring second-order beneficiaries and only adding the same-position handcuff, missing the receiver who inherits the targets. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Points-Allowed-by-Position, Regression-Aware (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Regression-Aware Points-Allowed-by-Position. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: How many fantasy points a defense surrenders to a position, shrunk toward league average to correct for the schedule of opponents it has already faced. INPUTS (general): raw fantasy points allowed by position, strength of offenses faced, sample size. HOW TO READ IT: A defense that looks soft only because it played strong offenses regresses toward neutral; a genuinely leaky unit stays soft after adjustment. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to rank matchups for start/sit and streaming; it beats raw points-allowed rankings, which are badly distorted by early-season schedule luck. COMMON MISTAKE: Trusting unadjusted defense-versus-position tables in the first weeks, when one or two opponents dominate the sample. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Touchdown-Dependence Flag (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Touchdown-Dependence Flag. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The share of a player's fantasy scoring that comes from touchdowns rather than yardage and receptions, indicating how fragile his weekly floor is. INPUTS (general): touchdown share of total points, yardage and reception baseline, red-zone role. HOW TO READ IT: High touchdown dependence means boom-or-bust variance and likely regression after a hot run; low dependence means a stable, volume-backed floor. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to choose floor plays for must-win weeks and to time sell-high windows; it beats season points-per-game, which hides how the points were earned. COMMON MISTAKE: Penciling in a touchdown-dependent player for repeat scoring after a multi-touchdown game without yardage to support it. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Committee Backfield Read (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Committee Backfield Read. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a multi-back room splits early-down, passing-down, and goal-line work, mapping which back owns the fantasy-relevant slices. INPUTS (general): per-back snap split by down type, passing-down usage, goal-line carry share. HOW TO READ IT: The back who owns passing downs has a points-per-reception floor; the goal-line back owns touchdown equity; a true even split caps everyone's ceiling. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to value the right back in a timeshare for start/sit; it beats treating a committee as one startable name, which mis-ranks each piece. COMMON MISTAKE: Starting the touches leader while the goal-line and passing-down splits hand the scoring to a teammate. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: In-Season Bye-Week Pre-Planning (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: In-Season Bye-Week Pre-Planning. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The roster stress from upcoming bye weeks at each position, used to schedule cheap streamer adds before the crunch arrives. INPUTS (general): upcoming bye distribution by position, current positional depth, waiver replacement quality. HOW TO READ IT: A week where several of your starters share a bye is a planned shortfall to pre-empt; a position with built-in depth needs no action. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to add bye-week fill-ins a week or two early at a discount; it beats scrambling on the same morning everyone else is, when the streamer pool is picked clean. COMMON MISTAKE: Holding a bench bye-stack too long and being forced to overbid for a starter on the shortfall week. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Floor vs Ceiling Start Logic (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Floor vs Ceiling Start Logic. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether to prioritize a player's safe expected output or his upside, conditioned on whether the matchup requires a steady score or a big swing. INPUTS (general): projection mean, projection spread/variance, the week's win condition (favored vs underdog). HOW TO READ IT: When projected to win, favor floor and lower-variance players; when projected to lose, favor ceiling and high-variance players who can swing the week. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to set lineups against a known opponent total rather than in a vacuum; it beats always starting the highest mean projection regardless of game state. COMMON MISTAKE: Playing for the ceiling in a game you are already favored to win, adding needless variance to a likely victory. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: In-Season Lineup Correlation (Stacking) (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: In-Season Lineup Correlation. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The degree to which two of your own starters' scores move together because they share a game, which raises the variance of your weekly team total. INPUTS (general): same-game pairings on your roster, positive pairings (quarterback with his pass-catcher), negative pairings (opposing players). HOW TO READ IT: Positive same-team stacks amplify both ceiling and floor; rostering opposing players partly cancels their swings; correlation matters more when you need a big or a safe week. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to deliberately raise or lower team variance to fit the matchup; it beats setting a lineup as independent slots, which ignores how your scores co-move. COMMON MISTAKE: Unknowingly stacking a quarterback against your own receiver, flattening your team's ceiling when you needed it. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Vulture / Goal-Line Back Risk (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Vulture / Goal-Line Back Risk. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The risk that a teammate steals short-yardage and goal-line scores from an otherwise high-volume back, capping his touchdown ceiling. INPUTS (general): inside-the-five carry split, short-yardage personnel package, recent goal-line usage trend. HOW TO READ IT: A back who moves the ball but cedes the finish has a yardage floor but suppressed touchdown equity; owning the goal-line role is the touchdown driver regardless of total touches. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to discount a volume back's ceiling and to value the vulture as a touchdown-dependent flex; it beats ranking backs by total touches alone. COMMON MISTAKE: Projecting touchdowns for the touches leader when a designated short-yardage back actually finishes the drives. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Coverage-Shadow (CB Matchup) for Receivers (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Coverage-Shadow Matchup for Receivers. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The expected suppression of a receiver who is likely to be followed by an elite shutdown cornerback across the formation, versus a receiver who avoids that travel. INPUTS (general): opponent shadow-corner tendency, the receiver's alignment (perimeter vs slot), the corner's coverage strength. HOW TO READ IT: A perimeter receiver shadowed by a top corner faces a real downgrade; a slot or motion-heavy receiver often escapes the shadow and keeps his projection. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use to fine-tune receiver start/sit beyond team-level defense ratings; it beats using a defense's overall pass rank, which misses player-specific travel. COMMON MISTAKE: Benching a slot-heavy receiver for a shadow corner who only travels with outside receivers. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Pace-of-Play Matchup (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Pace-of-Play Matchup. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points, in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The expected number of offensive plays in a game, driven by both teams' tempo, which scales the raw opportunity available to every skill player. INPUTS (general): each team's neutral-pace play rate, expected pass rate, projected game competitiveness. HOW TO READ IT: Two fast, pass-leaning teams in a close game inflate everyone's volume; a slow, run-heavy, blowout-prone pairing deflates it; pace multiplies, not replaces, per-play role. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Use as a volume multiplier on top of usage for start/sit and streaming; it beats per-game averages, which assume a fixed number of plays. COMMON MISTAKE: Stacking a high-usage player into a slow, grind-it-out game and expecting his usual touch count. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Trade Value as Rest-of-Season Starting-Lineup Delta (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Rest-of-Season Starting-Lineup Delta. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: The true value of a trade is the change in points your OPTIMAL STARTING lineup scores over the remaining schedule, not the change in total roster talent. WHAT IT MEASURES: It isolates the marginal points that actually reach your scoreboard each week. INPUTS (general): projected rest-of-season production for incoming and outgoing players; your current weekly starter at each affected position; remaining number of games. HOW TO READ IT: Compute your projected starting lineup before and after the trade across the remaining weeks; the difference is the real gain or loss. Points you add to the bench count for nothing. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the accept/reject decision on any trade offer. Beats the naive baseline of comparing raw player rankings or season-long totals, which credits bench depth you never start. COMMON MISTAKE: Counting a player's full projection when he would only displace an already-strong starter, so most of his points sit on your bench. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Two-for-One Consolidation Logic (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Two-for-One Consolidation. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether trading two roster players for one better player improves your STARTING output, given that only a fixed number of slots score each week. INPUTS (general): combined starter value of the two outgoing players; value of the single incoming player; quality of the bench replacement that fills the vacated roster spot. HOW TO READ IT: A two-for-one helps the side that consolidates when the single star out-scores the WORSE of the two given-up players plus whatever bench piece backfills the open slot. The giver wins on roster depth, the receiver wins on top-end ceiling. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves consolidation trades, especially for contenders who need a higher weekly ceiling. Beats the naive baseline of summing total player value on each side, which ignores that you must replace the open roster spot. COMMON MISTAKE: Forgetting that the consolidating side opens a roster hole that a waiver or bench player must fill, eroding the apparent gain. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Positional Value Asymmetry in Trades (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Positional Value Asymmetry. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: How the same nominal point value is worth more or less depending on the position's scarcity and replacement level, so trades across positions are rarely one-for-one in real value. INPUTS (general): position-specific replacement level (points available off waivers at each position); positional depth on your roster; starting-slot requirements of your league. HOW TO READ IT: Convert each player to points-above-replacement at HIS position before comparing. A point at a scarce position is worth more than a point at a deep one, so the same raw projection trades unequally across positions. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves cross-position trades (e.g., RB for WR). Beats the naive baseline of comparing projected points directly, which treats all positions as interchangeable. COMMON MISTAKE: Trading away a scarce-position starter for a deep-position player of equal projection, leaving a hole waivers cannot fill. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Buy-Low Window After a Bad Game (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Buy-Low Window. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: The temporary gap between a player's depressed perceived value after one or two poor outings and his stable underlying expectation, creating an acquisition discount. INPUTS (general): underlying usage signals (snaps, targets, touches) versus recent fantasy output; whether the bad games were caused by game-script or matchup rather than role loss; the owner's emotional reaction or frustration. HOW TO READ IT: When opportunity volume holds steady but points dipped, the market overreacts and the player can be bought below true value. A drop in actual ROLE, not luck, means the discount is real and not a bargain. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the timing of buy offers. Beats the naive baseline of valuing players by recent box-score points, which chases results instead of process. COMMON MISTAKE: Buying low on a player whose underlying role genuinely collapsed (lost job, snap share gone), mistaking decline for variance. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Sell-High Window After a Spike (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Sell-High Window. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: The temporary premium on a player's perceived value after an unsustainable big game, when his market price exceeds his stable forward expectation. INPUTS (general): how much of the spike came from low-probability events (long touchdowns, garbage time) versus repeatable usage; forward role and target/touch trend; the buying market's recency bias. HOW TO READ IT: When a spike was driven by efficiency or touchdowns that exceed his usual usage, sell into the inflated demand. When the spike reflects a permanent ROLE increase, the value is real and holding is correct. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the timing of sell offers. Beats the naive baseline of holding any player who just scored big, which ignores regression to underlying volume. COMMON MISTAKE: Selling high on a player whose spike was actually a role change (new target hog), giving away ascending value. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Package-Value Curvature (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Package-Value Curvature. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: The non-linearity of player value, where two good players are worth less than one great player because only the best pieces start and the rest sit, so value curves upward at the top. INPUTS (general): the steepness of the value-versus-rank curve at the relevant tier; the number of startable slots available; the depth of the bench discount. HOW TO READ IT: Because top-tier value rises faster than rank, combining two mid players does not equal one elite player; the elite tier carries a scarcity premium. Packaging makes sense only when the curve is locally flat. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves structuring package deals to acquire elite talent. Beats the naive baseline of additive value math (two 70s equal one 140), which ignores the convex top of the curve and bench dead-weight. COMMON MISTAKE: Assuming player values add linearly and over-paying with quantity when the league only starts a few elite pieces. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Contender vs Pretender Trade Posture (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Contender vs Pretender Posture. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether your team's realistic playoff odds justify a win-now posture (pay for ceiling) or a depth/rebuild posture (bank floor and assets). INPUTS (general): current record and playoff-probability estimate; roster ceiling versus the field; remaining schedule difficulty. HOW TO READ IT: High playoff odds favor trading depth for a higher weekly ceiling, since you must beat strong opponents in the playoffs. Marginal or low odds favor consolidating for floor or accumulating future/keeper value. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the strategic stance behind every trade. Beats the naive baseline of always maximizing raw roster value regardless of standings, which leaves contenders too flat and pretenders over-invested. COMMON MISTAKE: A team on the playoff bubble acting like a lock and dealing away the depth that keeps it alive through byes and injuries. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Playoff-Schedule-Weighted Trade Value (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Playoff-Schedule-Weighted Value. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: A player's trade value weighted toward the fantasy playoff weeks specifically, since those games decide the championship and matter more than regular-season filler weeks. INPUTS (general): the NFL strength-of-matchup a player faces during the fantasy playoff weeks; the player's bye relative to those weeks; expected role stability into late season. HOW TO READ IT: Up-weight players who face soft defenses during your league's title weeks and down-weight those who hit tough matchups or a bye then. A great regular-season player with a brutal playoff slate is worth less to a contender. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves contenders making mid-season trades. Beats the naive baseline of season-long average value, which treats week 5 and championship week as equally important. COMMON MISTAKE: Acquiring a star who is on bye or faces elite defenses precisely during your championship week. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Bye-Week-Driven Trade Timing (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Bye-Week Trade Timing. SPORT: Fantasy Football (snake/points; trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: How bye-week clustering on a roster temporarily distorts a team's needs and creates short-term trade leverage in both directions. INPUTS (general): which weeks each roster has stacked byes at a position; the immediacy of the upcoming bye crunch; depth available to cover the gap. HOW TO READ IT: A team facing a near-term bye crunch at a position will overpay for short-term coverage; a team with no crunch can sell that coverage at a premium. Bye distortions fade, so do not pay long-term value for a one-week patch. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the timing and framing of trade offers around byes. Beats the naive baseline of valuing players by season totals, which ignores the leverage created by a clustered bye week. COMMON MISTAKE: Trading away a quality player permanently just to survive a single bye week you could have patched off waivers. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Keeper Cost vs Value (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Keeper Cost vs Value. SPORT: Fantasy Football (keeper decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether a player is worth keeping by comparing the draft-pick or auction price you pay to retain him against his expected draft-market value next season. INPUTS (general): the keeper cost (round or auction dollars to retain); the player's projected draft-market value entering next season; positional replacement level at that cost. HOW TO READ IT: A keeper is profitable when his expected value clearly exceeds the cost you surrender to keep him; the bigger the surplus, the stronger the keep. A player kept at roughly his market price provides no edge. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the keep/release decision for each candidate. Beats the naive baseline of keeping your best players outright, which ignores that an expensive keeper cost can erase the advantage. COMMON MISTAKE: Keeping a star at a steep cost when the surplus over his market price is negligible, wasting the keeper slot. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Keeper Opportunity Cost (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Keeper Opportunity Cost. SPORT: Fantasy Football (keeper decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: The value of the player you FORGO at the draft slot consumed by a keeper, since keeping a player at a given round means you cannot use that pick on a fresh player. INPUTS (general): the draft slot the keeper occupies; the expected player available at that slot if not spent on the keeper; the keeper's surplus over that forgone player. HOW TO READ IT: A keeper is only worth it if his value exceeds the BEST player you would otherwise draft at that pick, not merely his own market price. The relevant comparison is keeper minus forgone draftee. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves allocating keeper slots across competing candidates. Beats the naive baseline of evaluating each keeper in isolation, which ignores the pick you sacrifice. COMMON MISTAKE: Keeping a good player at an early pick while overlooking that the same pick could have landed an even better fresh draftee. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Keeper Inflation Across Seasons (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Keeper Inflation. SPORT: Fantasy Football (keeper decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: How removing kept players from the draftable pool inflates the cost of remaining talent, because the league drafts from a shallower pool of available players. INPUTS (general): the number and quality of players kept league-wide; the resulting thinness of the available draft pool; your draft or auction budget relative to that pool. HOW TO READ IT: When many strong players are kept, the remaining draftable players cost more than their raw value, so nominal prices rise across the board. Plan draft or auction strategy against the post-keeper inflated pool, not the full-league baseline. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves draft-budget and keep-vs-release planning in keeper leagues. Beats the naive baseline of valuing the draft as if all players were available. COMMON MISTAKE: Anchoring auction or pick value to full-pool rankings and then overpaying because the kept players already removed the cheap talent. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Multi-Keeper Roster Construction (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Multi-Keeper Construction. SPORT: Fantasy Football (keeper decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: How to choose a SET of keepers jointly to maximize total surplus, given that keepers compete for slots and consume draft capital together. INPUTS (general): the surplus value of each keeper candidate; the draft picks each one consumes; positional balance the kept set leaves on the roster. HOW TO READ IT: Pick the combination that maximizes aggregate surplus subject to the slot and pick constraints, not just the individually best players. A balanced set that fills multiple positions can beat hoarding surplus at one spot. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves leagues that allow multiple keepers. Beats the naive baseline of independently ranking each keeper, which can over-commit picks or stack one position. COMMON MISTAKE: Keeping the highest-surplus players regardless of which draft rounds they cost, leaving no early picks to draft around them. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Dynasty-Startup vs Redraft Valuation Gap (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Dynasty vs Redraft Valuation Gap. SPORT: Fantasy Football (keeper/trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: The systematic difference in player value between dynasty (multi-year horizon) and redraft (single-season horizon), driven by how much future seasons count. INPUTS (general): the valuation horizon (one season versus many); the player's age and career trajectory; how much future production is discounted. HOW TO READ IT: Young ascending players carry a large dynasty premium and a smaller redraft value; aging producers are the reverse. The wider the horizon, the more youth and longevity outweigh present output. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves cross-format trades and converting between dynasty and keeper-league thinking. Beats the naive baseline of using one ranking set for both formats, which misprices age. COMMON MISTAKE: Applying redraft rankings in a dynasty context (or vice versa) and badly mispricing young players and veterans. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Rookie-Pick Valuation in Keeper Leagues (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Rookie-Pick Valuation. SPORT: Fantasy Football (keeper/dynasty trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: The trade value of future rookie draft picks, which are options on uncertain players and therefore valued by expected outcome and risk, not a fixed price. INPUTS (general): the expected production distribution of players typically available at that pick slot; the hit rate and bust risk at that range; your team's contender-vs-rebuild horizon. HOW TO READ IT: Early rookie picks carry option value and upside but real bust risk, so discount them below a known producer of equal expected output. Rebuilding teams value picks more; contenders value proven players more. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves trades involving rookie picks in keeper/dynasty formats. Beats the naive baseline of treating a pick as a guaranteed star or as worthless, both of which misprice the option. COMMON MISTAKE: A contender overpaying with proven players to acquire speculative rookie picks that will not help this season. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Age Cliff and Keeper Hold-or-Sell (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Age Cliff Hold-or-Sell. SPORT: Fantasy Football (keeper/trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: The timing of selling an aging player BEFORE his position's typical decline, since value erodes fast once the age cliff hits and the market reprices. INPUTS (general): the player's age relative to his position's known decline curve; current workload and efficiency trend; remaining keeper or dynasty horizon. HOW TO READ IT: Positions decline at different ages; a veteran approaching his position's cliff should be sold while perception still lags reality. Holding past the cliff means selling into a falling market. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the hold-versus-sell decision on veteran keepers. Beats the naive baseline of holding producers until output visibly drops, which guarantees you sell after the decline. COMMON MISTAKE: Keeping a beloved aging star one year too long and watching both his production and trade value collapse together. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Trade Fairness and Collusion-Perception (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Trade Fairness / League Health. SPORT: Fantasy Football (trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a trade's perceived fairness affects league approval, future trade partners, and overall league engagement, beyond the raw value to the two teams. INPUTS (general): the value imbalance perceived by the rest of the league; the standings context of both teams (e.g., a rebuilder feeding a contender); the league's veto or review norms. HOW TO READ IT: Even a privately fair trade can stall if the league reads it as lopsided or collusive; reputation and future deal-making depend on being seen as fair. Lopsided deals risk vetoes and unwilling future partners. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves structuring trades that clear league review and preserve relationships. Beats the naive baseline of optimizing only the two-team value, which ignores social and veto risk. COMMON MISTAKE: Pushing a technically savvy but optically lopsided deal that gets vetoed or poisons future negotiations. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Three-Team Trade Structuring (Fantasy Football)
body: CONCEPT: Three-Team Trade Structuring. SPORT: Fantasy Football (trade decision). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a three-way trade can unlock deals that no pairwise trade could, by routing each team's surplus to the team that needs it most. INPUTS (general): each team's surplus and need by position; the missing two-way overlap that blocks a direct deal; the net value each team gains. HOW TO READ IT: A three-team trade works when team A's surplus fits team C's need while team C's surplus fits team B and so on, completing a cycle that no single pair could close. Every team must end up net positive or the chain collapses. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves complex trades where two teams cannot match needs directly. Beats the naive baseline of only attempting two-team deals, which leaves mutually beneficial cycles unexploited. COMMON MISTAKE: Building a three-way deal where one leg is only marginally positive, so that team backs out and the whole structure unravels. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Football (concept only).

title: Punt Free-Throw Percentage Build (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Punt-FT% Build. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The competitive gain from conceding the free-throw-percentage category so that low-FT% big men become net positives rather than dead weight. INPUTS (general): player category contributions, free-throw volume profile, remaining-category strength after the punt. HOW TO READ IT: Once FT% is conceded, value the roster on the surviving categories only; targets that were penalized for poor FT shooting recover most of their true worth. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the decision to commit early to a punt structure; beats a balanced-build value list that systematically underrates high-volume, low-percentage centers. COMMON MISTAKE: Drafting a high-volume free-throw shooter anyway, which re-opens the conceded category and wastes the build's central trade-off. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Punt Field-Goal Percentage Build (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Punt-FG% Build. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The value unlocked by conceding field-goal percentage so that high-volume guards and chuckers stop dragging the roster down. INPUTS (general): player category contributions, shooting-volume profile, surviving-category strength. HOW TO READ IT: Evaluate candidates only on the remaining categories; guard-heavy scorers and three-point specialists rise because their FG% drag no longer counts. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the choice to anchor a guard-centric build; beats a balanced ranking that penalizes efficient-volume mismatch and undervalues perimeter scorers. COMMON MISTAKE: Mixing in a hyper-efficient big to chase FG% anyway, half-committing and weakening both the punt and the category you tried to keep. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Punt Assists Build (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Punt-Assists Build. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The roster flexibility gained by conceding assists, freeing the manager to load up on wings and bigs without paying for playmaking. INPUTS (general): player category contributions, playmaking dependence, surviving-category strength. HOW TO READ IT: Score players on every category except assists; non-creators like rebounding/blocks wings become premium because the build no longer needs lead guards. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves a frontcourt-heavy identity that stacks defense and efficiency; beats a balanced board that overpays for elite point guards to chase a single category. COMMON MISTAKE: Still spending up for a ball-dominant guard, paying an assist premium that the build explicitly chose not to need. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Punt Turnovers Build (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Punt-Turnovers Build. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The value reclaimed by conceding turnovers so high-usage stars stop being penalized for the cost-of-doing-business giveaways that come with volume. INPUTS (general): player category contributions, usage and ball-handling load, surviving-category strength. HOW TO READ IT: Ignore the turnover column; ball-dominant scorers and playmakers recover the value normally docked for high giveaway counts. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves a stars-and-usage build; beats a balanced ranking that punishes high-usage engines for turnovers inseparable from their production. COMMON MISTAKE: Treating turnovers as nearly free and ignoring that it is among the easiest categories to incidentally win, costing a punt that yields little. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Punt Points Build (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Punt-Points Build. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The contrarian edge from conceding total points so the manager can corner the defensive and efficiency categories with specialists nobody else values. INPUTS (general): player category contributions, scoring dependence, surviving-category density. HOW TO READ IT: Drop the points column; low-scoring stat-stuffers (stocks, boards, percentages) become cornerstone assets that competitors leave on the table. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves a deep-specialist identity in leagues where scoring is over-drafted; beats a board that anchors on points and ignores the cheap multi-category role players. COMMON MISTAKE: Underestimating that points correlates with several other categories, so a careless punt-points roster bleeds threes and free-throw makes too. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Category Scarcity Premium (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Category Scarcity Premium. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How concentrated the supply of a category is across the player pool, identifying which stats (typically blocks and steals) come from few sources and thus command a premium. INPUTS (general): leaguewide distribution of each category, number of viable suppliers, depth past the starter tier. HOW TO READ IT: Categories sourced from a thin handful of players are scarce; securing them early is harder to replace than counting stats spread across many players. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves draft sequencing and price tolerance for scarce-category producers; beats a flat per-category value that treats an easily streamed stat the same as a thin one. COMMON MISTAKE: Waiting on a scarce category expecting late-round replacements that never materialize, leaving a permanent hole. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Multi-Category Specialist Value (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Multi-Category Specialist Value. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The roster efficiency of a player who supplies meaningful production in several categories at once, condensing needs into fewer lineup slots. INPUTS (general): per-category contribution spread, breadth of positive categories, slot opportunity cost. HOW TO READ IT: A player positive in many categories frees other slots to specialize, while a one-category spike forces compensating picks elsewhere. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves slot-allocation decisions in shallow rosters; beats a raw-total ranking that rewards a single huge category over balanced breadth. COMMON MISTAKE: Overvaluing breadth so much that the roster has no elite category and loses close matchups for lack of a decisive edge anywhere. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Stars-and-Scrubs vs Balanced Budget Allocation (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Stars-and-Scrubs vs Balanced Budget. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (auction; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The trade-off between concentrating budget into a few elite anchors versus spreading it for a deep, even roster. INPUTS (general): budget concentration profile, top-end ceiling, roster depth requirement. HOW TO READ IT: Concentration buys ceiling and category dominance but thins the back end; balance buys floor and matchup resilience at the cost of true stars. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the overall auction allocation strategy; beats a uniform spend that ignores how league depth and category structure reward one shape over the other. COMMON MISTAKE: Going stars-and-scrubs without a streaming plan, so injuries or off-nights from the cheap tail collapse the lineup. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Nomination Strategy (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Nomination Strategy. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (auction; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The tactical use of who you put up for bid to drain rival budgets and shape the market before nominating players you actually want. INPUTS (general): opponent remaining budget, opponent positional and category needs, your own target list timing. HOW TO READ IT: Nominate players you do not want but rivals do to spend down their dollars; introduce your targets when competitors are cash-constrained. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the sequencing of bids in an auction; beats naively nominating your own favorites first and inflating their price against full-pocket opponents. COMMON MISTAKE: Nominating a player you secretly want as a price-discovery test and getting stuck winning him at a price you never intended. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Budget Pacing Through an Auction (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Budget Pacing. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (auction; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether your spend rate tracks the value still on the board, so you neither run dry early nor leave dollars stranded at the end. INPUTS (general): dollars remaining, roster slots remaining, value remaining in the pool. HOW TO READ IT: Compare your cash-per-remaining-slot against the value still available; overspending early signals a thin endgame, underspending signals leftover dollars with nothing to buy. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves continuous mid-auction discipline; beats a fixed shopping list that ignores how the live market has shifted prices. COMMON MISTAKE: Hoarding budget so conservatively that the auction ends with unspent dollars and replacement-level fill-ins. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Last-Dollar Endgame Value Spots (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Last-Dollar Endgame Value. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (auction; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The systematic surplus available late in an auction when most managers are budget-constrained and useful players clear at minimum or near-minimum bids. INPUTS (general): late-auction budget distribution, remaining player quality, your reserved dollars. HOW TO READ IT: If you hold a small budget reserve while rivals are tapped out, late nominations of rotation contributors return outsized value per dollar. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the decision to reserve flexible dollars for the endgame; beats spending the full budget on the top tiers and accepting forced minimum-bid scraps. COMMON MISTAKE: Over-reserving and missing the stars, then finding the late pool is also picked clean of the few useful bargains. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Value Over Replacement by Category (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Value Over Replacement by Category. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: A player's contribution measured against the freely available replacement level within each category separately, rather than against zero. INPUTS (general): per-category production, the replacement baseline for each category, roster and league size. HOW TO READ IT: Value is the gap above what you could grab off waivers for that stat; categories with high replacement baselines reward only the elite producers. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves cross-position and cross-category comparison of true draft value; beats raw category totals that credit a player for production easily replaced for free. COMMON MISTAKE: Setting one global replacement level instead of per-category, which mis-prices scarce-category producers. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Position Eligibility and Multi-Position Flexibility (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Multi-Position Flexibility Value. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The lineup-management premium of a player eligible at multiple positions, which eases daily slotting and lets you start more games. INPUTS (general): eligibility breadth, scarcity at the player's positions, lineup-slot structure. HOW TO READ IT: Multi-eligible players reduce the chance of benching production for lack of an open slot, effectively raising usable output. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves roster-construction and tiebreaker decisions between similar players; beats flat per-game projections that ignore how often a player can actually be slotted. COMMON MISTAKE: Paying a large premium for flexibility in shallow leagues where open slots are rarely the binding constraint. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Games-Played Durability Weighting (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Games-Played Durability Weighting. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H or points; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a player's expected availability discounts per-game value, since missed games are zero production regardless of talent. INPUTS (general): availability and injury history, age and load profile, role security. HOW TO READ IT: Multiply per-game value by expected availability; a fragile star and a durable role player can converge in real season-long worth. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the decision to discount injury-prone talent at draft; beats per-game rankings that assume full participation and overrate the chronically unavailable. COMMON MISTAKE: Over-discounting players on load-managed teams whose rest is predictable and plannable around, unlike random injury. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Schedule Density at Draft (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Schedule Density Weighting. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a team's games-per-week count over the season affects the cumulative usable production of its players in weekly head-to-head formats. INPUTS (general): team weekly game counts, light-week and heavy-week distribution, playoff-week schedule.
