HOW TO READ IT: Players on teams that play more games in key weeks, especially fantasy-playoff weeks, deliver more counting stats per roster slot. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves tiebreakers and late-round value in weekly leagues; beats per-game rankings that ignore how many games actually accrue in the weeks that decide titles. COMMON MISTAKE: Drafting heavily around full-season schedule totals while ignoring the specific fantasy-playoff weeks that matter most. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Punt-Build Synergy Target Lists (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Punt-Build Synergy Targets. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The reinforcement effect among players who all gain value under the same punt, so a build compounds rather than just tolerates its concession. INPUTS (general): chosen punt category, each player's recovered value under that punt, overlap in surviving-category strength. HOW TO READ IT: Stack players whose profiles all benefit from the same conceded category; their combined surviving-category output overwhelms balanced opponents there. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves cohesive target-list construction once a punt is chosen; beats picking individually cheap players whose strengths scatter across categories you are not contesting. COMMON MISTAKE: Stacking so narrowly that one category is dominated by a wide margin while several others quietly go uncontested. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Categorical Balance vs Spike Build (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Balance vs Spike Build. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The contrast between rosters built to be competitive in every category and rosters built to dominate a chosen subset while conceding others. INPUTS (general): per-category margin distribution, number of categories contested, opponent build tendencies. HOW TO READ IT: A spike build trades safe categories for guaranteed wins in others; a balance build aims to edge many categories narrowly with no guaranteed losses. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the top-level identity choice before drafting; beats treating every category as equally winnable when roster math forces concessions. COMMON MISTAKE: Attempting balance with limited resources and ending up mediocre everywhere, losing close matchups for want of any decisive category. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Snake ADP Value (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: ADP Value Gap. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The gap between a player's projected value rank and the market's average draft position, identifying where consensus mispricing creates value picks. INPUTS (general): your projection rank, market average draft position, positional run patterns. HOW TO READ IT: Players whose projection rank sits well ahead of their draft position are value targets; those drafted ahead of projection are traps to fade. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves pick timing and the choice to wait on a player likely to fall; beats reaching for personal favorites at picks earlier than the market requires. COMMON MISTAKE: Treating ADP as a hard ceiling and waiting too long, then losing a target to another manager who values him correctly. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Tier Construction by Category (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Tier Construction. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (snake or auction; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The grouping of players into tiers where the drop-off between tiers exceeds the spread within a tier, marking where a position or category becomes urgent. INPUTS (general): projected values within a position or category, the size of gaps between clusters, supply remaining in each tier. HOW TO READ IT: When a tier is nearly exhausted, the next pick at that need is urgent because the drop to the following tier is steep; otherwise you can safely wait. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves live pick-urgency decisions; beats a flat ranked list that gives no signal about when waiting becomes costly. COMMON MISTAKE: Drawing tier lines from raw rank order instead of from genuine value cliffs, producing false urgency. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Late-Round Upside Targeting (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Late-Round Upside Targeting. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (snake or auction; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The expected payoff of using low-cost late picks on breakout candidates whose ceiling far exceeds their floor, rather than safe known quantities. INPUTS (general): opportunity-change signals (role, depth chart, minutes), ceiling-to-floor spread, cost of the pick. HOW TO READ IT: Late in a draft the downside of a bust is small while the upside of a breakout is large, so variance is an asset not a liability. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the back-half-of-draft selection philosophy; beats filling late slots with safe veterans whose capped output rarely swings a season. COMMON MISTAKE: Loading the entire bench with lottery tickets and leaving no reliable plug-in starters for early weekly needs. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Rookie Valuation (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Rookie Valuation. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (snake or auction; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: The expected fantasy contribution of a first-year player, accounting for opportunity and role uncertainty far wider than for established veterans. INPUTS (general): projected role and minutes, team context and depth ahead, profile of comparable past rookies. HOW TO READ IT: Weight opportunity over draft pedigree; a rookie with a clear path to minutes outproduces a higher-pedigree rookie buried on the depth chart. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the decision of when and how high to draft unproven talent; beats valuing rookies on hype or NBA-draft position rather than fantasy-relevant role. COMMON MISTAKE: Anchoring on preseason buzz and ignoring that most rookies start slow before role and efficiency stabilize. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Source-of-Scoring Concentration Risk (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Scoring-Source Concentration Risk. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How dependent a player's fantasy value is on a single stat source, which makes the value fragile to a small change in role or shot selection. INPUTS (general): share of value from each category, dependence on a single skill, volatility of that source. HOW TO READ IT: A player whose value is dominated by one fragile source (for example three-point makes) carries more bust risk than one with diversified production. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves risk assessment when comparing similarly ranked players; beats a point-estimate ranking that ignores how brittle the underlying production is. COMMON MISTAKE: Treating a one-source spike player as interchangeable with a diversified producer of the same projected total. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Free-Throw-Volume Sourcing (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Free-Throw-Volume Sourcing. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a player's free-throw attempt volume, not just percentage, drives both the makes counting stat and the leverage of his percentage on team totals. INPUTS (general): free-throw attempt volume, free-throw accuracy, team-level percentage leverage. HOW TO READ IT: High-volume accurate shooters anchor the percentage category by weight, while high-volume poor shooters can sink it; low-volume players barely move it either way. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves both percentage-category planning and punt-FT% targeting; beats reading FT% in isolation without the attempt volume that determines its impact. COMMON MISTAKE: Picking up a great-percentage but low-volume shooter expecting to move the team percentage meaningfully. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Usage-Driven Floor (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Usage-Driven Floor. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H or points; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a high offensive workload underwrites a stable production floor, since heavy involvement produces stat-stuffing nights even when efficiency dips. INPUTS (general): offensive usage rate, ball-handling and creation role, multi-category footprint. HOW TO READ IT: Players with secure high usage rarely post zeros across the board, giving a dependable weekly floor and triple-double upside. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the search for reliable early-round anchors; beats efficiency-only rankings that prize percentage over the volume that guarantees a floor. COMMON MISTAKE: Assuming usage transfers automatically to a new team or role when it actually depends on the surrounding depth chart. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Minutes-Security at Draft (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Minutes-Security Weighting. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H or points; auction or snake; draft-day). WHAT IT MEASURES: How safe a player's playing time is from competition, coaching whim, or a crowded depth chart, since per-minute talent only pays off with the minutes to express it. INPUTS (general): depth-chart standing, coaching rotation tendencies, competition for the role. HOW TO READ IT: A talented player with a contested role carries hidden downside; a lesser talent with locked minutes can be the safer real-value pick. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves tiebreakers between similar players and the fading of role-risk talents; beats per-minute or per-game projections that assume minutes are guaranteed. COMMON MISTAKE: Chasing a high per-minute breakout candidate stuck behind an entrenched starter, then waiting all season for minutes that never open. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Games-Played Leverage (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Games-Played Leverage. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: How much extra category or point output a roster can capture in a given scoring period purely by maximizing the number of player-games started, before any talent difference is considered. INPUTS (general): weekly team schedule density, active roster slot count, per-player baseline production rate. HOW TO READ IT: A roster that fields more games than its opponent banks counting-stat volume even with weaker players; the leverage is the spread in startable games, not the spread in talent. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves the weekly start/sit decision; beats the naive habit of starting your best names regardless of how many games they actually play that week. COMMON MISTAKE: Treating a high-talent player on a light schedule as a must-start when a replacement-level player with more games delivers more total volume. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Streaming for Games Played (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Streaming for Games Played. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The marginal counting-stat gain from cycling free agents through open roster slots specifically to add games on nights when rostered starters are idle. HOW TO READ IT: The value of a streamer is dominated by whether he plays on an otherwise-empty night, not by his per-game ceiling; a mediocre player on a busy night beats a star who is off. INPUTS (general): nightly slate of which rostered players are active, free-agent availability and their game nights, transaction or add limits. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves daily add/drop in deep leagues; beats holding a static roster and leaving slots empty on heavy slates. COMMON MISTAKE: Streaming a name you like on a night you are already full, wasting a transaction without adding any games. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Schedule-Aware Weekly Lineup (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Schedule-Aware Weekly Lineup. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The optimal allocation of limited active slots across a week so that high-value players occupy slots on their game nights and bench congestion is minimized. INPUTS (general): each player's game nights across the period, total active slots, daily versus weekly lineup lock rules. HOW TO READ IT: The lineup is a scheduling problem over the week, not a single snapshot; the goal is zero wasted player-games due to slot collisions. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves leagues with daily lineup setting; beats setting a lineup once and never revisiting it as nightly slates change. COMMON MISTAKE: Locking a star into a slot early in the week and being forced to bench another quality player on a shared game night. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Matchup Category Targeting (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Matchup Category Targeting. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: Which categories in a given weekly head-to-head are realistically winnable and worth concentrating resources on, versus which are conceded by default. INPUTS (general): your projected category totals, opponent's projected category totals, the closeness of each category gap. HOW TO READ IT: Categories cluster into near-locks, true tossups, and near-losses; the tossups are where lineup and streaming effort changes the outcome. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves pre-week and mid-week category strategy; beats trying to win every category at once and spreading effort thin. COMMON MISTAKE: Pouring streamers into a category you were already winning comfortably instead of the contested middle band. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Mid-Matchup Category Clinch (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Mid-Matchup Category Clinch. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The point in a weekly matchup at which a category lead is mathematically or practically unreachable by the opponent given remaining games, so further investment is wasted. INPUTS (general): current category margin, opponent's remaining games and ceiling, your remaining games. HOW TO READ IT: Once a category is clinched, every additional resource spent there is dead weight that should be redirected to contested categories. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves mid-week reallocation; beats continuing to start specialists in a category you have already locked. COMMON MISTAKE: Failing to recognize a clinch and leaving a low-volume specialist active when those slots could chase a tossup category. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Mid-Matchup Category Punt (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Mid-Matchup Category Punt. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The point at which a category is unrecoverable this week, so it should be abandoned live and its supporting slots reassigned to still-winnable categories. INPUTS (general): current deficit in the category, opponent's remaining ceiling, the opportunity cost of slots tied up chasing it. HOW TO READ IT: A lost category is worth the same whether you lose it by a little or a lot, so concede cleanly and convert effort into categories on the bubble. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves live in-matchup triage; beats stubbornly chasing a category you cannot win and bleeding effort from winnable ones. COMMON MISTAKE: Streaming hard for a category already out of reach because the deficit feels close, rather than redirecting to a true tossup. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Punt-Aware Add/Drop (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Punt-Aware Add/Drop. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The value of a free agent evaluated only against the categories your build actually competes in, ignoring production in your punted categories. INPUTS (general): your team's active category set, the candidate's production within those categories, the candidate's cost to punted categories. HOW TO READ IT: A player who is generically valuable but loads up your punted categories can be a poor fit, while a narrow specialist in your live categories is a strong add. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves waiver decisions for committed punt builds; beats using a generic all-category ranking to pick up players. COMMON MISTAKE: Adding the highest-ranked available player when his strengths are concentrated in categories you have intentionally given up. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Minutes and Usage Spike Detection (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Minutes and Usage Spike Detection. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: An early signal that a rostered or available player is about to receive a durable increase in role, distinguished from a one-off spurt. INPUTS (general): recent trend in minutes and shot or possession share, the cause of the change such as an injury ahead of them, the depth chart context. HOW TO READ IT: A spike backed by a structural cause and sustained minutes is a buy signal; a spike from foul trouble or blowout garbage time is noise. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves proactive waiver claims before a player is widely owned; beats reacting only after a big box score has already spread. COMMON MISTAKE: Chasing a single inflated game whose minutes and usage have no durable cause behind them. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Blowout-Risk Minutes Downgrade (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Blowout-Risk Minutes Downgrade. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The expected reduction in a starter's minutes and counting stats when his game is likely to be a lopsided result and starters sit late. INPUTS (general): projected game competitiveness or spread, the player's role as a starter versus closer, the team's tendency to rest in blowouts. HOW TO READ IT: A starter in a likely blowout carries a haircut on his ceiling even if the matchup looks soft on paper. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves start/sit and streamer selection; beats picking streamers purely on a soft defensive matchup without accounting for game script. COMMON MISTAKE: Streaming a player into an apparently easy matchup that projects as a runaway, costing fourth-quarter minutes. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Back-to-Back and Rest Risk (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Back-to-Back and Rest Risk. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The probability that a player sits or has minutes capped on the back end of consecutive game nights, and the resulting effect on his weekly game count. INPUTS (general): the team's back-to-back nights in the period, the player's age and load-management profile, his durability history. HOW TO READ IT: A player nominally on a four-game week may effectively be a three-game player if a back-to-back sit is likely. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves weekly volume planning and roster lock decisions; beats counting scheduled games as if every one will be played. COMMON MISTAKE: Penciling in a veteran's full schedule and being surprised by a planned rest night on the second of a back-to-back. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Free-Agent Category Fit (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Free-Agent Category Fit. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: How well an available player's category profile aligns with your current roster's specific weaknesses rather than his standalone overall value. INPUTS (general): your roster's per-category strength and shortfall, the candidate's category shape, scarcity of the candidate's strong categories on the wire. HOW TO READ IT: The best add is the one that patches your scarcest contested categories, even if a higher-ranked generalist is available. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves targeted waiver pickups; beats always grabbing the top remaining player by overall ranking. COMMON MISTAKE: Adding another player who reinforces a category you already dominate instead of one who fills a thin category. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Stash vs Stream Tradeoff (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Stash vs Stream Tradeoff. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether a roster spot is better spent holding an injured or buried player for future upside or cycling streamers through it for immediate weekly production. INPUTS (general): the stash candidate's expected return timeline and upside, the current weekly value of a streamed slot, your standing and urgency. HOW TO READ IT: Stashing trades present games for a future payoff; the trade is worth it only when the upside and your timeline both justify the lost current production. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves bench management; beats reflexively holding every intriguing name or reflexively streaming every slot. COMMON MISTAKE: Stashing multiple long-term upside plays while in a must-win window that needs current weekly volume. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Injury-Return Ramp (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Injury-Return Ramp. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The discounted production expected from a player in his first games back from injury while he is on a minutes restriction before reaching full role. INPUTS (general): the nature of the injury and expected restriction length, the team's stated ramp plan, the player's pre-injury role. HOW TO READ IT: A returning player is worth less than his healthy baseline during the ramp window and should be valued on restricted minutes, not full minutes. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves start/sit and acquisition timing on returning players; beats slotting a returnee straight back into a full-volume role. COMMON MISTAKE: Starting a just-returned player at his old projection and getting capped, low-minute lines for a week or two. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Role-Change Opportunity (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Role-Change Opportunity. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The fantasy upside created when a player moves into a meaningfully different role, such as a starting promotion, a position change, or a new offensive responsibility. INPUTS (general): the trigger such as a trade, injury, or lineup change, the new role's typical opportunity profile, the player's fit for it. HOW TO READ IT: Value follows opportunity, so a role change can lift a fringe player above many rostered names overnight even without a skill change. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves anticipatory waiver claims around lineup and depth-chart shifts; beats valuing players only on their season-long averages. COMMON MISTAKE: Waiting for the new role to show up in box scores before claiming, by which point the player is gone. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Category Consistency by Standard Deviation (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Category Consistency by Standard Deviation. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: How game-to-game variable a player's output is within each category, separating steady contributors from boom-or-bust producers. INPUTS (general): a player's distribution of per-game results within a category, the shape of that spread, his floor relative to his average. HOW TO READ IT: A high-variance contributor helps when you need a swing to flip a tossup but hurts when you need a reliable floor to protect a narrow lead. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves matchup-specific start/sit when you are favored versus when you need upside; beats treating two players with equal averages as interchangeable. COMMON MISTAKE: Starting a boom-or-bust player to protect a lead, or a steady floor player when you need a ceiling to come from behind. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Weekly Category Projection vs Opponent (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Weekly Category Projection vs Opponent. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: A forward projection of each category's final weekly total for both you and your opponent, used to forecast the category-by-category outcome before the week resolves. INPUTS (general): both rosters' remaining games, per-player category rates, expected lineup usage. HOW TO READ IT: The projection reveals the likely final category ledger and surfaces which categories are still in play, anchoring every in-week decision. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves planning the whole week and re-planning mid-week; beats reacting only to the live scoreboard without a forecast of where it ends. COMMON MISTAKE: Reading the current scoreboard as the outcome when one side has many more games remaining. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: In-Season Punt-Build Maintenance (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: In-Season Punt-Build Maintenance. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: How well a roster stays committed to its punted categories over the season, avoiding drift that dilutes the build's structural advantage. INPUTS (general): the roster's intended punt set, the category profiles of recent adds, the cumulative shift in category strengths. HOW TO READ IT: Each add or drop should preserve the punt; accumulated off-build pickups quietly erode the edge that punting was meant to create. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves season-long roster discipline; beats making waiver moves on standalone value while the build identity slowly degrades. COMMON MISTAKE: Drifting back toward a balanced roster by adding good all-around players, surrendering the concentrated advantage in your live categories. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Last-Roster-Spot Churn (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Last-Roster-Spot Churn. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The cumulative value gained by treating the final bench spot as a rotating resource cycled for the best available short-term play rather than a fixed hold. INPUTS (general): the marginal value of the current holder, the best streaming or matchup option available, transaction limits. HOW TO READ IT: The last spot has low holding value, so its worth comes from frequent reuse for games, matchups, or speculative upside. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves continuous bench optimization; beats letting a low-value player occupy the final spot all season. COMMON MISTAKE: Holding a familiar but replaceable name in the last spot instead of churning it for weekly schedule and matchup edges. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Counting-Stat Sourcing When Behind (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Counting-Stat Sourcing When Behind. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: Where remaining attainable volume in a contested counting category can be sourced from when you trail, given your remaining games and available specialists. INPUTS (general): the size of the deficit, your remaining game count, the wire's supply of specialists in that category. HOW TO READ IT: Closing a counting-stat gap requires either more games or sharper specialists; if neither can cover the deficit, the category should be conceded instead. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves comeback planning in close categories; beats vague hope that current rostered players will erase a gap on their own. COMMON MISTAKE: Assuming a counting deficit will close itself without auditing whether the remaining games can actually supply the needed volume. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Percentage-Category Protection (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Percentage-Category Protection. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The impact a player has on a ratio category like field-goal or free-throw percentage weighted by his attempt volume, not just his raw percentage. INPUTS (general): the player's shooting percentage in the category, his attempt volume, your current standing in that ratio category. HOW TO READ IT: A high-volume poor shooter can sink a percentage category, while a low-volume player barely moves it; volume is the lever, not the rate alone. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves start/sit and streaming decisions that affect ratios; beats judging shooters by their percentage without regard to attempts. COMMON MISTAKE: Starting a high-attempt inefficient scorer in a week where you are defending a narrow percentage lead. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Streaming Without Hurting Percentages (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Streaming Without Hurting Percentages. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The percentage-category risk introduced by a streamer added for counting stats or games, so volume gains do not silently cost you a ratio category. INPUTS (general): the streamer's shooting efficiency, his attempt volume, the closeness of your percentage categories this week. HOW TO READ IT: A streamer is only free if his attempt volume cannot meaningfully drag your ratio categories; an inefficient high-volume streamer can win a counting category and lose two percentages. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves daily streaming in category leagues; beats streaming purely for counting volume while ignoring ratio collateral. COMMON MISTAKE: Adding an inefficient gunner for points or boards and tanking field-goal percentage in a week it was contested. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Off-Night Schedule Penalty (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Off-Night Schedule Penalty. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The reduction in a roster's effective weekly capacity caused by many of its players sharing the same game nights, leaving light nights with no startable options. INPUTS (general): the distribution of player game nights across the week, active slot count, how concentrated games are on heavy nights. HOW TO READ IT: A roster clustered on a few nights wastes slots on those nights and fields nobody on light nights, lowering total games below its nominal schedule. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves roster construction and streaming to flatten the nightly distribution; beats judging a roster only by total scheduled games. COMMON MISTAKE: Building a roster heavy on the same game nights and being unable to fill slots on sparse league nights. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: In-Season Category-Need Trade (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: In-Season Category-Need Trade. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The value of a trade judged by how it rebalances your category profile toward your contested needs, trading from a surplus category to shore up a deficit. INPUTS (general): your category surpluses and shortfalls, the partner's complementary needs, the category shape of the players exchanged. HOW TO READ IT: A good in-season trade can lose raw overall value yet win more weekly matchups by converting a wasted surplus into a contested category. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves mid-season roster rebalancing; beats evaluating trades only by aggregate player ranking or total value. COMMON MISTAKE: Rejecting a trade because you give up the higher-ranked player while ignoring that it fixes a category that costs you matchups. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Fantasy-Playoff Week Schedule Planning (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Fantasy-Playoff Week Schedule Planning. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The advantage gained by favoring players whose teams have strong schedules during the fantasy-playoff weeks, including game counts and back-to-back load. INPUTS (general): team schedules in the target playoff weeks, game density and rest spots, the player's expected availability. HOW TO READ IT: A player's playoff-week schedule can outweigh small talent gaps, since a four-game week beats a two-game week of a slightly better player. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves pre-playoff roster shaping and acquisition targeting weeks in advance; beats optimizing only for the current week with no look-ahead. COMMON MISTAKE: Entering the fantasy playoffs with stars stuck on light or back-to-back-heavy schedules in the decisive weeks. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Load-Management Read for Stars (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Load-Management Read for Stars. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (H2H category or points; in-season). WHAT IT MEASURES: The likelihood that a high-usage veteran sits a given game for maintenance rest, and the resulting expected weekly game count for that star. INPUTS (general): the player's age and injury history, the team's rest patterns and standings incentives, the schedule's back-to-back and travel spots. HOW TO READ IT: A star's expected weekly value should be discounted for predictable rest games, and contingency streamers prepared for the nights he is likely out. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Serves weekly volume forecasting and bench contingency planning; beats assuming a star plays every scheduled game. COMMON MISTAKE: Leaving a slot empty on a likely rest night instead of pre-positioning a streamer to cover the star's absence. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Category-Fit Trade (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Category-Fit Trade. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (trade/keeper). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether a proposed trade improves the categories you can actually still win, rather than whether it raises your total roster value. INPUTS (general): your live-category standing, the cats each side gives and gets, opponent roster shape. HOW TO READ IT: A trade that adds raw value but only in categories you have already locked or already lost is a wash; one that swaps surplus in a safe category for help in a contested one is a win even at flat total value. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Evaluating any in-season trade in a category league; beats total-value (z-sum) trade calculators that ignore which cats move your weekly wins. COMMON MISTAKE: Accepting the side with the higher aggregate value while your roster gets more lopsided. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Consolidation Trade for a Punt Build (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Consolidation Trade for a Punt Build. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (trade/keeper). WHAT IT MEASURES: The value of trading two or more mid-tier players for one star whose category profile reinforces the punt you are already committed to. INPUTS (general): your punt categories, the candidates' anti-fit with the punted cats, roster slots freed or consumed. HOW TO READ IT: The deal wins when the incoming star's weakness sits in your punted category and his strengths concentrate your live cats; a star who is strong in your punted cat wastes that strength. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Upgrading a committed punt roster mid-season; beats best-player-available consolidation that ignores whether the star fits or fights your punt. COMMON MISTAKE: Consolidating into a star whose profile contradicts your build identity. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Consolidation and the Freed Roster Slot (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Consolidation and the Freed Roster Slot. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (trade/keeper). WHAT IT MEASURES: The true cost of giving multiple players for one star, accounting for the roster slot you free and the replacement-level player who refills it from the wire. INPUTS (general): the outgoing profiles, the incoming profile, expected wire replacement quality. HOW TO READ IT: A many-for-one is only a win when the star plus a streamed replacement out-produces the players you gave, across your live categories; in shallow leagues the wire refill is strong and many-for-one deals favor the star side. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Deciding whether to consolidate; beats counting raw player value and forgetting the freed slot gets refilled. COMMON MISTAKE: Valuing the deal as star-minus-players and ignoring the replacement that fills the empty slot. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Buy-Low on Cold Shooting (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Buy-Low on Cold Shooting. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (trade/keeper). WHAT IT MEASURES: How much of a player's depressed FG%/FT% is noise likely to mean-revert toward his established baseline rather than a real decline. INPUTS (general): career and multi-season shooting baseline, recent attempt volume, any role or shot-diet change. HOW TO READ IT: A short cold streak on stable volume and shot profile is mostly variance and a buy-low window; a cold stretch that coincides with a worse shot diet or reduced role is a real signal, not noise. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Targeting undervalued shooters in trade; beats reacting to recent percentages as if a small sample were the new true rate. COMMON MISTAKE: Treating a few weeks of bad percentages as a permanent talent drop. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Sell-High on Unsustainable Usage (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Sell-High on Unsustainable Usage. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (trade/keeper). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether a hot stretch is propped up by a temporary usage or minutes spike that will recede when a teammate returns or rotation normalizes. INPUTS (general): cause of the spike (injury absence, blowout minutes), the player's baseline role, return timeline of the displaced teammate. HOW TO READ IT: Production riding a soon-to-end opportunity bump is a sell-high; production from a durable role change (trade, promotion) is real and should be held. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Timing when to ship a surging player at peak perceived value; beats holding every hot player until the regression has already happened. COMMON MISTAKE: Mistaking a teammate-injury minutes spike for a genuine breakout. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Schedule-Weighted Trade Value (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Schedule-Weighted Trade Value. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (trade/keeper). WHAT IT MEASURES: A player's rest-of-season or playoff-window value adjusted for how many games his team plays in the weeks that matter, not just per-game rate. INPUTS (general): remaining team game counts by week, fantasy-playoff week schedule, back-to-back density. HOW TO READ IT: Two players of equal per-game value diverge when one's team plays four games and the other two in a key week; for keepers and deadline buys, weight the playoff-week game totals heaviest. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Trade and start/sit decisions tied to a weekly format; beats ranking by per-game rate as if every player logged the same number of games. COMMON MISTAKE: Ignoring game-count when the format scores weekly totals. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Keeper Cost vs Category Value (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Keeper Cost vs Category Value. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (trade/keeper). WHAT IT MEASURES: A keeper's surplus as his projected category value minus the draft cost or round it takes to retain him, expressed against what that pick would otherwise return. INPUTS (general): keeper price (round or salary), projected value next season, expected value of the pick spent. HOW TO READ IT: A keeper is worth holding when projected value clears the cost of the pick or salary by a meaningful margin; a star kept at an early-round price near his market value is roughly neutral, not a bargain. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Deciding which players to retain; beats keeping the best raw player regardless of what his retention price costs you. COMMON MISTAKE: Keeping a star at a price that erases all his surplus over the pick. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Keeper for a Punt-Build Cornerstone (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Keeper for a Punt-Build Cornerstone. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (trade/keeper). WHAT IT MEASURES: A keeper's value measured inside the punt build you intend to run next season, not on a balanced full-category baseline. INPUTS (general): your intended punt categories, the keeper's profile within those punts, his retention cost. HOW TO READ IT: A player who is mediocre on a balanced board but elite once a punt cancels his weakness is a far better keeper than his global rank suggests; his anti-fit cat becomes free. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Selecting keepers when you already know your build direction; beats ranking keepers by global all-category value blind to your build. COMMON MISTAKE: Passing on a punt cornerstone because his standard-league rank looks ordinary. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Win-Now vs Rebuild Trade Posture (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Win-Now vs Rebuild Trade Posture. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (trade/keeper). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether your category standings and playoff odds justify trading future/keeper value for immediate help, or banking present surplus for next season. INPUTS (general): current playoff probability, gap to a playoff spot, keeper or dynasty value of assets. HOW TO READ IT: A team with real title odds should pay future value for win-now category fixes; a team out of contention should sell aging present value for keeper-eligible youth. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Setting your whole deadline strategy; beats trading every deal on flat present-value with no posture, which leaves contenders timid and lost teams overpaying for now. COMMON MISTAKE: Buying win-now help when math says you are eliminated, or selling when you are a live contender. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Trade-Deadline Category-Standings Read (Fantasy Basketball)
body: CONCEPT: Trade-Deadline Category-Standings Read. SPORT: Fantasy Basketball (trade/keeper). WHAT IT MEASURES: In roto or season-long category formats, which categories are within reach of gaining standings points and which are stranded, so deadline moves target movable points. INPUTS (general): your per-category rank, the point gaps to teams above and below, games remaining. HOW TO READ IT: A category where you trail the next team by a closeable margin is worth buying into; one stranded mid-pack with no reachable team above is dead weight to acquire for. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Directing deadline trades at standings points you can actually catch; beats improving categories abstractly without checking which point gaps are closeable. COMMON MISTAKE: Spending assets to pad a category whose standings rank cannot change. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Regression to the Mean (Fantasy)
body: CONCEPT: Regression to the Mean. SPORT: Fantasy (general, football & basketball). WHAT IT MEASURES: How much of an extreme recent stretch is noise that will drift back toward the player's established baseline, versus a real change in talent or role. INPUTS (general): established multi-season baseline, recent sample size, whether the underlying opportunity changed. HOW TO READ IT: The smaller the sample and the more luck-driven the stat (percentages, touchdown rate, three-point variance), the harder it regresses; a shift in role or usage moves the baseline itself and does not regress. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Pricing buy-low and sell-high windows; beats extrapolating a hot or cold streak as the new true rate. COMMON MISTAKE: Treating a small-sample spike as a permanent new level. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Floor vs Ceiling and Roster Role (Fantasy)
body: CONCEPT: Floor vs Ceiling and Roster Role. SPORT: Fantasy (general, football & basketball). WHAT IT MEASURES: Which end of a player's outcome distribution matters given the role he fills on your roster -- a safe floor for a must-start core spot, a high ceiling for a swing or upside lottery spot. INPUTS (general): the player's outcome distribution, your roster need (anchor vs dart), the format's payout shape. HOW TO READ IT: A high-floor player is more valuable than a higher-ceiling one in a spot you cannot afford a bust; the upside player wins in a spot where you need a tournament-style spike. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Slotting players to roles and start/sit; beats ranking everyone by mean projection regardless of where they sit on your roster. COMMON MISTAKE: Starting a boom-bust player in a slot that needed a reliable floor. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Marginal Value and Opportunity Cost (Fantasy)
body: CONCEPT: Marginal Value and Opportunity Cost. SPORT: Fantasy (general, football & basketball). WHAT IT MEASURES: The value of a move as the gain over the next-best alternative for the same slot or resource, not the raw value of the player or pick acquired. INPUTS (general): the candidate's value, the value of the best alternative for that slot, the cost spent. HOW TO READ IT: A high-value add is only a marginal win if it clears whatever you would otherwise have put in that slot; an add over a near-equal alternative is close to free value forgone. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Every add, trade, and draft pick; beats counting acquired value in isolation while ignoring what was given up or displaced. COMMON MISTAKE: Celebrating a strong add that barely beats the player it replaced. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Age-Curve Discounting (Fantasy)
body: CONCEPT: Age-Curve Discounting. SPORT: Fantasy (general, football & basketball). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a player's projection should be nudged up or down for where he sits on his position's aging curve, especially for keeper and dynasty horizons. INPUTS (general): player age, position-specific aging shape, signs of early decline or late ascent. HOW TO READ IT: A player on the rising side of the curve carries upside beyond last year's line; one past the position's peak should be discounted even if recent production looks intact. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Keeper retention and multi-year trade value; beats projecting forward from last season flat with no aging adjustment. COMMON MISTAKE: Paying full price for an aging player on the strength of a stat line that is about to decline. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Injury-Risk Discounting (Fantasy)
body: CONCEPT: Injury-Risk Discounting. SPORT: Fantasy (general, football & basketball). WHAT IT MEASURES: A player's expected value adjusted for the probability and severity of missed time, converting a per-game rate into a realistic full-season expectation. INPUTS (general): injury history and chronic-risk flags, position and workload exposure, expected games available. HOW TO READ IT: A high per-game player with heavy missed-time risk can be worth less than a durable lower-ceiling player once availability is priced in; risk also widens the outcome band. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Valuing players for drafts, keepers, and trades; beats ranking on per-game production as if availability were guaranteed. COMMON MISTAKE: Paying a healthy-season price for a player with a chronic availability problem. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Name-Brand and Draft-Capital Bias Guard (Fantasy)
body: CONCEPT: Name-Brand and Draft-Capital Bias Guard. SPORT: Fantasy (general, football & basketball). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether a valuation is inflated by a player's reputation, past stardom, or high real-league draft pedigree rather than his current projected production and role. INPUTS (general): current projected production, current role and opportunity, reputation or pedigree separate from output. HOW TO READ IT: When market price sits well above projected role-driven value, the gap is name premium and a sell or fade; an unheralded player matching the same projection is the better buy at a discount. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Trade and draft valuation; beats paying for the name on the jersey or the rookie draft slot instead of the current opportunity. COMMON MISTAKE: Trading up for a famous name whose role no longer supports the price. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Sunk-Cost Guard in Drops (Fantasy)
body: CONCEPT: Sunk-Cost Guard in Drops. SPORT: Fantasy (general, football & basketball). WHAT IT MEASURES: Whether a player earns his roster spot on rest-of-season expectation alone, with the draft cost or trade price already paid treated as irrecoverable and irrelevant. INPUTS (general): the player's rest-of-season projection, the best available alternative for that slot, current need. HOW TO READ IT: A high pick who has busted should be judged only against the wire alternative going forward; the capital spent to acquire him is gone and must not protect his roster spot. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Cut and drop decisions; beats clinging to expensive acquisitions because of what they cost rather than what they will return. COMMON MISTAKE: Holding a busted early pick over a clearly better waiver option to avoid admitting the loss. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Correlation and Stacking (Fantasy)
body: CONCEPT: Correlation and Stacking. SPORT: Fantasy (general, football & basketball). WHAT IT MEASURES: How the outcomes of two rostered players move together, so a lineup's variance and ceiling reflect joint behavior, not just summed individual projections. INPUTS (general): shared game or team context, whether players feed the same production source, format payout shape. HOW TO READ IT: Positively correlated pieces (a passer and his pass-catcher, teammates whose pace lifts together) raise both ceiling and bust risk; negatively correlated or independent pieces smooth variance for a safe build. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Tournament-style lineup construction and managing roster variance; beats treating players as independent and summing projections blind to correlation. COMMON MISTAKE: Stacking correlated pieces in a format that rewards a steady floor, or vice versa. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Format Translation of Player Value (Fantasy)
body: CONCEPT: Format Translation of Player Value. SPORT: Fantasy (general, football & basketball). WHAT IT MEASURES: How a player's value shifts when the same production is scored under a different format -- points vs category vs roto, PPR vs standard, weekly vs season-long. INPUTS (general): the player's production profile by stat type, the target format's scoring weights, roster and matchup rules. HOW TO READ IT: A volume reception back gains in PPR and loses in standard; an efficient specialist gains in category and loses in points; a player's rank is format-specific, not absolute. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Reading rankings or trade values imported from a different format; beats applying one universal ranking across leagues with different scoring. COMMON MISTAKE: Using a points-league ranking to run a category league, or PPR ranks in a standard league. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).

title: Small-Sample Caution In-Season (Fantasy)
body: CONCEPT: Small-Sample Caution In-Season. SPORT: Fantasy (general, football & basketball). WHAT IT MEASURES: How much trust an early-season or short-run trend has earned, given how few games inform it and how noisy the stat is. INPUTS (general): number of games in the sample, the stat's inherent volatility, the player's prior expectation. HOW TO READ IT: Early in a season a player's true level is dominated by the preseason prior; the sample only overrides it as games and consistency accumulate, faster for stable stats than for volatile ones. WHEN TO USE IT / WHAT IT BEATS: Reading early-season breakouts and busts; beats over-trusting a few games as if the new rate were settled. COMMON MISTAKE: Declaring a breakout or a decline off a handful of games. SOURCE: Resolve internal / Wonka Resolve (concept only).
